subject: linear-algebra
title: Linear systems, elimination, rank & nullity
introduction: Gaussian elimination is not just a solving algorithm. Its pivots expose rank, free variables, consistency, and the entire geometry of a linear system in one pass.
theory: Elementary row operations preserve the solution set. In echelon form, pivots identify basic variables and non-pivot columns correspond to free variables.
A system $Ax=b$ is consistent exactly when $b$ lies in the column space of $A$, equivalently when $rank(A)=rank([Amid b])$.

examples.title: Free variables
examples.solution: Nullity is $5-3=2$, so a homogeneous solution uses two free parameters.

examples.title: Inconsistency row
examples.solution: This represents $0=2$, so no solution exists.

examples.title: Unique solution
examples.problem: $A$ is square and has a pivot in every column.
examples.solution: $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$, so nullity zero and $Ax=b$ has a unique solution for every $b$.

examples.title: Same row space
examples.problem: $B$ is obtained from $A$ by row operations.
examples.solution: Row operations preserve row space dimension and rank, though they generally change the column space itself.

pitfalls: Using number of rows instead of number of columns in rank-nullity.
Saying row operations preserve the column space.
Calling a consistent system unique without checking free variables.
whyGate: Rank and solvability control regression uniqueness, redundant features, inverse problems, and low-dimensional representations.
